lines.s10: Meunier is Champagne's third grape, a black one, and it gives the blend ripe pear, red apple and an early, easy charm.
lines.s20: Meunier is the third grape of Champagne, a black grape pressed gently for white juice. It brings ripe pear, yellow plum and a soft, round middle, and it makes a Champagne ready to enjoy young.
lines.s45: Meunier is the third grape of Champagne, beside Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. It is a black grape, and its home is the Marne Valley, where it buds late and so suffers less from spring frost. In the glass it gives ripe pear, yellow plum and a little wild strawberry, with a soft, round feel. Most of it is pressed gently for white juice and blended, to fill out the middle of a Champagne that is ready young. A few growers bottle it alone. Pour it with fried chicken, mushrooms or a plate of charcuterie. Its name means miller, for the white down that dusts its leaves like flour.
lines.sale: Meunier is the grape that makes Champagne easy to love on the first sip: ripe pear, soft bubbles, nothing sharp. Start the table with a glass of it and the fried oysters.

glass.lead: Ripe pear, yellow plum and wild strawberry on a soft, round frame, with brioche from its time on the lees.

ladder.where: Champagne's Marne Valley, England, Tasmania and the Willamette Valley
Württemberg's sheltered Neckar valley, as a soft still red

glass.structure: Made as Champagne it is dry, with high acidity, moderate alcohol, a light to medium body and barely any tannin.

home.home: Champagne, above all the clay soils of the western Marne Valley, where late budding makes it less prone to spring frost. It is pressed gently for white juice and blended with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, to give ripe pear and a round middle to wines made to be enjoyed young. A few growers bottle it alone.
home.abroad: England grows it for sparkling wine made the Champagne way, and so do Tasmania and Oregon's Willamette Valley. In Germany it is Schwarzriesling or Müllerrebe, mostly in Württemberg, and is made as a light still red.

service.temp: 46 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as Champagne.
service.glass: A tulip shaped sparkling glass or a white wine glass, so the fruit can show.
service.decant: Rarely, and only if the guest asks; the bubbles are the point.
service.age: Wines led by Meunier tend to mature sooner than those led by Chardonnay or Pinot Noir; enjoy them young.

with.why: acidity and bubbles cut the brine and the batter
bubbles and acidity lift salt and fat
the wine's soft fruit sits well with mushrooms

labels.means: White Champagne from black grapes alone: Pinot Noir, Meunier or both.
The older name for the same grape; Champagne's own trade body writes Meunier.
The German name, black Riesling, though it is no relation of Riesling; also Müllerrebe.

guest.q: I only know Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. What is Meunier?
guest.a: It is the third grape of Champagne, a black grape and a natural mutation of Pinot Noir. It gives a blend its soft, ripe pear fruit, and many Champagnes include it.

guest.q: If the grape is black, why is the wine white?
guest.a: The colour is in the skins and the juice runs clear. Champagne presses whole bunches gently and takes the juice away before the skins can tint it.

guest.q: Is a Champagne with a lot of Meunier a lesser wine?
guest.a: No, a different one. It tends to be rounder and more open when young and to mature sooner, which is what many tables want.

compare.tell: Pinot Noir gives Champagne more body, structure and red cherry depth and ages longer; Meunier is softer, rounder and ready sooner.
Chardonnay brings Champagne lemon, chalk and long life; Meunier brings ripe pear, yellow plum and a supple middle.

profile.st: Black grape, mostly pressed white for sparkling wine · Body light to medium · Acid high · Tannin negligible · Alcohol moderate · Dry
profile.fruit: Ripe pear, red apple, yellow plum; wild strawberry and raspberry in rosé and still red
profile.other: Brioche and bread dough from lees ageing, hazelnut and dried mushroom with age; a soft, supple texture
profile.tell: The round, forward middle of a Champagne blend: soft and ready young, where Pinot Noir is firmer and Chardonnay leaner
profile.regions: Champagne (the Marne Valley above all), England, Württemberg in Germany (as Schwarzriesling), Tasmania, Willamette Valley
profile.confuse: Pinot Noir is firmer, with more red cherry and structure; Chardonnay is leaner, with lemon and chalk

cards.front: Meunier: which region is home, and what does it add to a blend?
cards.back: Champagne, above all the Marne Valley. It adds ripe pear and yellow plum fruit and a soft, round middle, in wines ready to enjoy young.

cards.front: Why does Meunier suit the frost prone clay soils of the Marne Valley?
cards.back: It buds later than Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, so spring frost harms it less, and it copes with soils that hold more clay.

cards.front: What does the name Meunier mean, and what is the grape's German name?
cards.back: Miller: its young leaves and shoot tips look dusted with flour. In Germany it is Schwarzriesling or Müllerrebe, grown mostly in Württemberg.

questions.q: A guest points to Blanc de Noirs on a Champagne label and asks which grapes it can be made from. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Blanc de Noirs is white Champagne from black grapes alone, which means Pinot Noir, Meunier or both. Chardonnay alone would be Blanc de Blancs.

questions.q: A sparkling wine is poured blind: ripe pear and yellow plum, soft and round, open and easy while still young. Which Champagne grape most likely leads the blend?
questions.exp: Supple wines of ripe pear and yellow plum that show early are the mark of Meunier. Chardonnay tends to be leaner and more chalky, and Pinot Noir firmer and more structured.

questions.q: A German wine list offers a light red called Schwarzriesling from Württemberg. Which grape is in the bottle?
questions.exp: Schwarzriesling, also Müllerrebe, is the German name for Meunier. Despite the name it is no relation of Riesling; it is a mutation of Pinot Noir.
